generic: Amphotericin B (conventional deoxycholate and lipid/liposomal formulations)
quick: Conventional (deoxycholate) 0.3-1.5 mg/kg/day IV; Liposomal (AmBisome) 3-6 mg/kg/day IV - NOT mg-for-mg interchangeable
IV only - not relevant (oral form for GI candidiasis only)
Drug of choice for serious systemic mycoses when needed; relatively safe
Generally avoid breastfeeding during systemic therapy
Nephrotoxic; reduce/space dose, hydrate; liposomal is less nephrotoxic
Renal function, electrolytes (K+, Mg2+), CBC, LFTs, infusion reactions
summary: Amphotericin B is a fungicidal polyene for severe systemic fungal infections. CRITICAL: conventional deoxycholate (Fungizone) and lipid/liposomal products are NOT interchangeable mg-for-mg - conventional is dosed ~0.3-1.5 mg/kg/day while liposomal AmBisome is 3-6 mg/kg/day (up to 5-6 mg/kg for some infections). Nephrotoxicity, infusion reactions, and electrolyte wasting are the dominant toxicities; lipid formulations reduce nephrotoxicity. Infuse only in 5% dextrose, never saline, with infusion-reaction precautions.
indications: Life-threatening systemic fungal infections: disseminated candidiasis, aspergillosis, cryptococcosis (incl. meningitis), histoplasmosis, blastomycosis, coccidioidomycosis, mucormycosis
Empirical antifungal therapy for presumed fungal infection in febrile neutropenia (liposomal)

dosage.d: Test dose 1 mg, then 0.25-0.3 mg/kg/day, increasing to 0.5-1.0 mg/kg/day (up to 1.5 mg/kg/day or alternate-day)
dosage.t: Once daily IV infusion over 2-6 h
dosage.n: Highly nephrotoxic; total course often months
Higher doses better tolerated than conventional

dosage.d: 3 mg/kg/day on days 1-5, and days 14 and 21 (total 21 mg/kg)

admin: WARNING: Conventional and lipid/liposomal amphotericin B are NOT interchangeable on a mg-per-mg basis - confirm the exact product and dose to avoid fatal dosing errors
Reconstitute and dilute ONLY in 5% dextrose (D5W) - never in saline (causes precipitation); do not mix with other drugs
Flush an existing IV line with D5W before infusing, or use a separate line
Conventional deoxycholate: a 1 mg IV test dose is often given; infuse slowly (commonly over 2-6 h) and monitor for acute infusion reactions
Liposomal/AmBisome: infuse over ~120 minutes (may shorten to ~60 min if tolerated); an in-line filter pore size must be >=1.0 micron
Pre-medicate (antipyretic/antihistamine +/- hydrocortisone) and pre-hydrate with saline to reduce infusion reactions and nephrotoxicity
moa: Amphotericin B binds ergosterol in the fungal cell membrane, forming pores that increase membrane permeability and cause leakage of intracellular potassium and other constituents, leading to fungal cell death (fungicidal). Lower-affinity binding to cholesterol in human cell membranes underlies its toxicity, including nephrotoxicity.

absolute: Known hypersensitivity to amphotericin B (unless the infection is life-threatening and no alternative exists)
relative: Pre-existing renal impairment (prefer a lipid formulation)

preg: Amphotericin B is considered the antifungal of choice for serious systemic mycoses in pregnancy; it crosses the placenta but has a relatively reassuring safety record. Use when clearly indicated.
lact: It is not known how much is excreted in milk; because of poor oral absorption infant exposure is likely low, but breastfeeding is generally avoided during systemic therapy.
renal: Dose-related nephrotoxicity is the major toxicity - it causes azotaemia, renal tubular acidosis and potassium/magnesium wasting. Pre-hydrate with saline, avoid other nephrotoxins, monitor renal function, and prefer lipid/liposomal formulations in those at risk; reduce or interrupt dosing for rising creatinine.
hepatic: Hepatotoxicity (raised enzymes/bilirubin) can occur; monitor liver function and use caution in hepatic impairment.

major: Other nephrotoxic drugs (aminoglycosides, ciclosporin, tacrolimus, contrast, NSAIDs) - additive renal injury
Skeletal muscle relaxants (e.g. tubocurarine) - hypokalaemia enhances curariform effect
moderate: Antineoplastic agents - enhanced renal toxicity, bronchospasm, hypotension
Leucocyte transfusions - acute pulmonary reactions reported
Flucytosine - amphotericin-induced renal impairment can raise flucytosine toxicity (also synergistic antifungal effect)
interactions.food: Not applicable - given intravenously (oral form acts locally in the gut only).
interactions.diagnostics: Causes raised creatinine/urea, hypokalaemia, hypomagnesaemia, anaemia and abnormal LFTs.

serious: Acute kidney injury / renal tubular acidosis
rare: Acute pulmonary toxicity (especially with leucocyte transfusions)
emergency: Cardiac arrest from rapid administration or severe hypokalaemia

monitoring: Renal function (creatinine, urea) at baseline and frequently during therapy
Serum potassium and magnesium - replace aggressively
CBC and liver function tests periodically
Vital signs during infusion for infusion-related reactions
Confirm correct product (conventional vs lipid/liposomal) and dose at every administration
counsel: This is a strong antifungal given by a drip in hospital for serious infections
Fever, chills and shaking during or after the infusion are common and can be treated
Blood tests will check your kidneys and salts (potassium/magnesium) regularly
Tell staff about any other kidney-affecting medicines you take
Report rash, breathlessness, palpitations, reduced urine output or severe infusion reactions
pk: Fungicidal action begins with infusion; clinical response over days
End-of-infusion plasma peaks; liposomal achieves higher plasma levels than conventional
Conventional terminal ~15 days (tissue-bound); liposomal differs by dose
Store powder refrigerated (2-8 C), protected from light; reconstitute only in D5W and use per stability limits
pearls: CRITICAL: never confuse conventional deoxycholate (~0.3-1.5 mg/kg/day) with lipid/liposomal (3-6 mg/kg/day) - they are NOT interchangeable mg-for-mg and dosing errors can be fatal
Reconstitute and infuse ONLY in 5% dextrose - saline causes precipitation
Nephrotoxicity and potassium/magnesium wasting dominate; pre-hydrate with saline and replace electrolytes
Lipid/liposomal formulations are less nephrotoxic and allow higher doses
Pre-medicate and slow the infusion for fever/rigor infusion reactions; watch digoxin toxicity from hypokalaemia
missed: Amphotericin B is given as scheduled inpatient/clinic infusions by healthcare staff, so patients do not self-administer doses. A missed or delayed infusion should be rescheduled by the treating team; do not attempt to make up doses by increasing the rate.
overdose: Overdose can cause cardiorespiratory arrest. There is no specific antidote and it is not removed by haemodialysis. Stop the drug, give cardiopulmonary and supportive care, monitor renal and cardiac function and electrolytes (especially potassium), and resume only after the patient's clinical status is reassessed.
